structure.heading: 13.1.1 Principles for Preparing the Sustainability Stateme nt [BP-1] [BP-2]
structure.start_phrase: The consolidated sustainability statement of Bank P ekao S.A. Capital Group (hereinafter: “Pekao Group” ) has been prepared in accordance with the Accounting Act of 29 Septemb er 1994, as well as the provisions of Regulation (E U) 2020/852 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2 020 on establishing a framework to facilitate susta inable investment.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and basis: Presents Bank Pekao S.A. Group’s consolidated Sustainability Statement for 2024, prepared under Poland’s Accounting Act, EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852, and ESRS per Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772; first year reporting under ESRS (previously GRI).
- Reporting scope and period: Covers the full Pekao Group on a fully consolidated basis for 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024, aligned with financial statements and encompassing the entire upstream and downstream value chain.
- Data and methodology choices: No omissions of information (e.g., IP or know‑how), no deviations from ESRS medium‑ and long‑term time horizons; metrics exclude value chain estimates derived from indirect sources. Includes forward‑looking information based on assumptions about climate and transition risks and opportunities, with associated uncertainties.
- External assurance: Limited assurance performed by PwC in line with Polish National Assurance Standards (3002; 3000(Z)) and ISAE 3000 (revised).
- Group composition: Parent Bank Pekao and subsidiaries/indirect subsidiaries across banking, asset management, brokerage, advisory, leasing, factoring, call‑center, transfer agent, cards, and insurance services. Entities named include Pekao Bank Hipoteczny, Centrum Kart, Pekao Direct, Pekao Faktoring, Pekao Financial Services, Pekao Investment Banking, Pekao Investment Management and Pekao TFI, Pekao Leasing and PEUF, as well as entities in liquidation/no operational activity (Pekao Fundusz Kapitałowy, Pekao Property incl. PB Media).
- Bank profile and oversight: Bank Pekao is a major Polish universal bank (assets > PLN 319bn), operating as a joint‑stock company under the Banking Law, Commercial Companies Code, and its Statute; supervised by KNF, listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange since 1998, part of PZU Group since 2017; headquarters in Warsaw (ul. Żubra 1).
- Governance framework and bodies:
  - General Meeting of Shareholders: Highest governing body; operates under the Commercial Companies Code and the Bank’s Statute; resolutions passed by absolute majority unless otherwise required.
  - Supervisory Board: Ongoing oversight; 7–9 members elected by the GMS for a joint 3‑year term. As of 31 Dec 2024: 8 members (87.5% men, 12.5% women), 75% independent; Chair not part of executive management; can form committees/teams. Members listed: Artur Olech (Chair), Bartosz Grześkowiak (Deputy Chair), Artur Nowak‑Far (Deputy Chair), Krzysztof Czeszejko‑Sochacki, Magdalena Joanna Dziewguć, Radosław Niedzielski, Jacek Nieścior, Witold Walkowiak.

nodes.title: Role of Administrative, Management, and Supervisory Bodies [GOV-1]
nodes.heading: 13.1.2.1 Role of Administrative, Management, and Supervisory Bodies [GOV-1]
nodes.start_phrase: Both Bank Pekao and its Group entities have an orga nisational structure tailored to their size and bus iness profile.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and legal framework: Bank Pekao S.A. is Poland’s second-largest universal bank (assets > PLN 319 billion), regulated by KNF, listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange since 1998, part of PZU Group since 2017, operating as a joint-stock company under the Banking Law Act, Commercial Companies Code, and the Bank’s Statute; headquarters in Warsaw (ul. Żubra 1).  
- Corporate governance structure: Responsibilities and competencies of bodies defined by law, supervisory recommendations, and internal statutes; organizational structure aligned to size and profile.  
- General Meeting of Shareholders (GMS): Highest governing body; operates per law and Statute; resolutions by absolute majority unless otherwise provided.  
- Supervisory Board: Ongoing oversight; 7–9 members elected for a joint 3-year term; as of 31.12.2024, eight members (87.5% men, 12.5% women), 75% independent; Chair not an executive; ability to form committees; full roster provided.  
- CSRD readiness: Supervisory Board has not yet fully identified competencies for managing impacts, risks, and opportunities (IRO); Audit Committee addresses sustainability topics; plan to upskill Supervisory Board in sustainability.  
- Management Board: Manages and represents the Bank; 5–9 members per term; in 2024 operated with nine, as of 31.12.2024 had six members (one woman); no employee representatives; declarations of no conflicts/competition/insolvency; Supervisory Board confirmed all members meet legal and internal suitability requirements.  
- Suitability policy and assessments: Bank applies a Selection and Suitability Assessment Policy (approved 30.12.2020) covering criteria, triggers, processes, and corrective measures for Management Board, Supervisory Board, and key function holders; in 2024 conducted initial, subsequent, and collective assessments; subsidiaries have aligned policies.  
- ESG governance and responsibilities: Management emphasizes ESG in governance, ethics, social/environmental initiatives, and human capital; Board is accountable for ESG report approval, sustainability risk management, legal compliance, and overseeing the sustainability reporting process.  
- ESG Council: Established in 2020 as an advisory/coordinating body for ESG and sustainability reporting; tasks include supporting ESG decisions, setting CSR/sustainability directions, guiding sustainable products, and reviewing subsidiaries’ ESG engagement; in 2024 did not cover material IRO, but in Dec 2024 its mandate expanded to monitor IRO management and approve double materiality results; objectives monitored by responsible unit directors; comprises four Management Board VPs plus key function representatives; meets at least quarterly.  
- Double materiality and next steps (GOV-2): First double materiality assessment completed in 2024 to identify key impacts, risks, and opportunities; ongoing work to build management mechanisms, systematic monitoring, policy effectiveness evaluation, indicators, and sustainability goals.

nodes.title: Information Provided to Administrative, Management, and Supervisory Bodies and Their Engagement in Sustainability Matters [GOV-2]
nodes.heading: 13.1.2.2 Information Provided to Administrative, Management, and Supervisory Bodies and Their Engagement in Sustainability Matters [GOV-2]
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, we conducted our first double materiality assessment, enabling us to identify key impacts, ri sks, and opportunities arising from our business activities.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Bank Pekao S.A. Group’s 2024 governance and oversight of ESG, emphasizing transparency in sustainability policies and reporting.
- The Management Board’s roles include approving ESG reports, overseeing risk management (including sustainability reporting risks), ensuring legal compliance, and managing the sustainability reporting strategy, procedures, and methodologies.
- The ESG Council (established 2020) coordinates ESG matters and sustainability reporting, supports decision-making, sets strategic CSR/sustainability directions, advises on sustainable products/services, and reviews subsidiaries’ ESG engagement. It meets quarterly and includes four Management Board members (responsible for risk, finance, corporate/markets/investment/business banking, retail/private banking) and key ESG function representatives.
- In 2024 the Council did not address material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IRO); in December 2024 its mandate was expanded to monitor IRO management and approve double materiality results. Sustainable development targets are monitored by responsible unit directors.
- The Bank conducted its first double materiality assessment in 2024, identifying key impacts, risks, and opportunities and initiating the development of management mechanisms, monitoring, and evaluation of policies, actions, indicators, and goals.
- The Management Board did not receive regular IRO reporting in 2024 but tracked selected strategy-linked areas: sustainable financing, client energy transition, climate neutrality actions, employee development and diversity, reducing the gender pay gap, social/environmental awareness, and high standards of governance and ethics.
- ESG risk and strategy reporting cadence:
  - Quarterly to the Management Board: utilization of the strategic ESG risk limit (Bank and Group) and progress on ESG Strategy KPIs; annually: self-assessment of compliance with ESG requirements. IRO aspects inform strategic oversight, risk decisions, and key environmentally positive financing decisions.
  - Quarterly to the ESG Council: key ESG risk indicators, accuracy of asset classification for ESG KPI calculations, progress on objectives/initiatives/KPIs, and regulatory compliance.
- The ESG Council analyzed climate mitigation/adaptation as risk factors and market opportunities. Key 2024 topics: monitoring strategic ESG risk indicators (notably transition risk tied to Scope 3, Category 15 emissions—Investments) and evaluating ESG KPI achievements; exploring opportunities in client transition products/services, reputation building, cooperation with development banks/investors, industry partnerships, and internal process effectiveness.
- Supervisory Board oversight includes reviewing Group Financial Statements and the Management Report with the Sustainability Statement, supported by three committees:
  - Audit Committee: oversees financial and sustainability reporting, internal control/risk/internal audit effectiveness, audit and assurance of sustainability reports, auditor independence, and communicates assurance outcomes to the Supervisory Board.
  - Nomination and Remuneration Committee: proposes Management Board contract/remuneration terms, Supervisory Board remuneration to the General Meeting, suitability assessments, and reports on remuneration policy effectiveness.
  - Risk Committee: evaluates current/future risk appetite, assesses the risk management strategy (credit/financial/operational), oversees implementation and pricing alignment with risk, and can receive direct input from risk management leaders.
- Incentives and sustainability performance:
  - The Remuneration Policy for Supervisory and Management Board members is governed, reviewed, and approved through defined bodies and cycles; aims include sound risk management, discouraging excessive risk, strategy support, conflict-of-interest mitigation, and gender-neutral pay.
  - Indicators align with long-term strategy and social/environmental commitments; sustainability risks are integrated into investment decisions.
  - Management Board variable remuneration includes a target to advance sustainable social development and integrate ESG; performance metrics include employee engagement, volunteering, financing sustainable projects, and digital/mobile progress. In 2024, these were not tied to specific IROs, and climate/GHG reduction targets were not embedded in variable pay.
  - Supervisory Board receives fixed pay only; Management Board variable pay is capped at 100% of prior-year fixed remuneration.
- Due diligence statement summarizes the Bank’s approach and references to sections covering: governance/strategy integration, stakeholder engagement, identification and assessment of adverse impacts, mitigation actions, and monitoring/reporting effectiveness.

nodes.title: Incorporating Sustainability Performance into Incentive Systems [GOV-3]
nodes.heading: 13.1.2.3 Incorporating Sustainability Performance into Incen tive Systems [GOV-3]
nodes.start_phrase: The remuneration strategy, developed in line with t he Bank’s operational standards, is reflected in in ternal regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Remuneration governance and policy for Bank Pekao S.A.’s Supervisory and Management Boards, including how sustainability performance is incorporated into incentives.
- Policy development and oversight process: drafted by the Management Board, reviewed by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee and the Risk Committee, approved by the Supervisory Board, and adopted by the General Meeting (at least every four years; significant changes require a new resolution).
- Policy objectives: promote sound risk management, curb excessive risk-taking beyond approved appetite, support business and risk strategies, mitigate conflicts of interest, and ensure gender‑neutral remuneration and employment conditions.
- Alignment of remuneration criteria with the Bank’s long-term strategy, considering social and environmental commitments, prevention/mitigation of negative social impacts, and integration of sustainability-related risks into investment decisions.
- Variable remuneration for Management Board Members includes ESG-oriented management targets (employee engagement, volunteering, financing sustainable projects, digital and mobile banking progress); however, in 2024 these were not tied to specifically defined material impacts/risks/opportunities, and climate/GHG reduction targets were not included.
- Remuneration structure: Supervisory Board—fixed monthly pay only; Management Board—fixed pay plus variable component tied to predefined targets (e.g., bank value, financial indicators), capped at 100% of the prior year’s fixed remuneration.
- Due diligence statement outlining key elements and cross-references within the sustainability statement: integration into governance/strategy/business model; stakeholder engagement; identification and assessment of adverse impacts; mitigation actions; and monitoring/reporting effectiveness, with specific section/page references provided.

nodes.title: Due Diligence Statement [GOV-4]
nodes.heading: 13.1.2.4 Due Diligence Statement [GOV-4]
nodes.start_phrase: Table 1: Due Diligence Elements
nodes.summary:
- Governance and remuneration: Detailed Remuneration Policy for Supervisory and Management Board members, including drafting, review, and approval by relevant bodies (Management Board, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, Risk Committee, Supervisory Board, General Meeting). Policy aims to promote sound risk management, prevent excessive risk-taking, support strategy, mitigate conflicts of interest, and ensure gender-neutral pay. Sustainability and ESG factors are embedded in remuneration criteria. Variable pay for Management Board links to employee engagement, volunteering, sustainable financing, and digitalisation/mobile banking; in 2024 it was not tied to specifically defined material impacts, risks and opportunities, nor to climate/greenhouse gas reduction targets. Supervisory Board receives fixed pay only; Management Board variable pay is capped at 100% of prior-year fixed pay and contingent on predefined targets.

- Due diligence: Overview of the due diligence process with cross-references to the Sustainability Statement covering governance integration, stakeholder engagement, impact identification/assessment, mitigation actions, and monitoring/reporting.

- Sustainability reporting controls: Internal assessment and control mechanisms to assure reporting quality and compliance; Management Board submission and Supervisory Board approval; annual internal audit review covering data verification, guideline compliance, and procedure effectiveness.

- Strategy and ESG: Description of broad banking operations (retail, corporate, private banking, asset management, brokerage) with strong capital/liquidity and high risk standards; customer-centric, integrated service model. 2021–2024 business strategy concluded in 2024; new strategy under development; continued execution of “Responsible Bank. Modern Banking” built on Customer, Growth, Efficiency, Responsibility pillars. ESG Strategy (2021–2024) “Responsible Bank Supporting Sustainable Development” extends the Responsibility pillar and is structured around:
  - Environment: financing sustainable projects, supporting energy transition and low-carbon shift, own carbon neutrality goal by 2030, participation in governmental/EU programmes.
  - Social Responsibility: initiatives for social/economic development, equal opportunities and inclusion, awareness/education, partnerships, and support for enterprise growth/innovation and digital payments.
  - Corporate Governance: ethical conduct with ESG considerations, promotion of development, diversity, equality and inclusion, transparency, and an attractive workplace through training and open dialogue.
  Note: ESG Strategy pillars are not directly linked to impacts, risks, and opportunities from the double materiality analysis.

- Business model and value chain: Customer-segmented model; Retail and Private Banking serve individuals (including HNWIs) and micro-enterprises via private banking centres, branches, partner outlets, and remote/digital channels.

nodes.title: Risk Management and Internal Controls in Sustainability Reporting [GOV-5]
nodes.heading: 13.1.2.5 Risk Management and Internal Controls in Sustainabi lity Reporting [GOV-5]
nodes.start_phrase: As part of our sustainability reporting management, we have established internal assessment and contro l mechanisms designed to ensure high quality and compliance of r eporting processes with applicable standards and be st market practices.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes governance and internal controls for sustainability reporting, including Management Board submission, Supervisory Board approval, and an annual internal audit reviewing data accuracy, compliance with guidelines, and process effectiveness.
- Describes Bank Pekao’s diversified operations in PLN and foreign currencies across domestic and international markets, offering corporate banking, private banking, asset management, and brokerage, supported by strong capital, liquidity, and risk management standards.
- Highlights a customer-centric, integrated service model with broad, innovative products aimed at strengthening market position; references statutory scope of activities.
- Notes conclusion of the 2021–2024 “Responsible Bank. Modern Banking” strategy in 2024, ongoing development of a new strategy, and delivery of objectives across four pillars: Customer, Growth, Efficiency, Responsibility.
- Presents the ESG Strategy “Responsible Bank Supporting Sustainable Development” (adopted 25 June 2021), aligned with the business strategy’s Responsibility pillar, structured into:
  - Environment: expand sustainable financing, support energy transition and low‑carbon economy, target Bank’s carbon neutrality by 2030, engage in government/EU recovery and climate programs.
  - Social Responsibility: advance societal and economic development, inclusion, and equal opportunities via assistance, awareness, education, partnerships; promote environmental awareness; support Polish enterprise growth and innovation, tech collaboration, and electronic/mobile payments.
  - Corporate Governance: uphold ethical business with ESG integration; promote development, diversity, equality, and inclusivity; ensure transparent policies and high governance standards; foster an attractive workplace with training, development, and open dialogue.

- Outlines the business model’s customer segmentation, detailing Retail and Private Banking for individuals (including high‑net‑worth clients) and micro‑enterprises, with investment advisory through private banking centers and remote channels, supported by branch and partner networks and digital platforms.

structure.title: Strategy, Business Model, and Value Chain [SBM-1]
structure.heading: 13.1.3.1 Strategy, Business Model, and Value Chain [SBM-1]
structure.start_phrase: At Bank Pekao, we conduct operations in both Polish zloty and foreign currencies, actively participati ng in domestic and international financial markets.
structure.summary:
- Governance of sustainability reporting: Bank Pekao has internal assessment and control mechanisms to ensure quality and compliance; sustainability reports are approved by the Management Board and Supervisory Board; internal audit performs an annual, in-depth review covering data verification, adherence to guidelines, and procedural effectiveness.

- Strategy overview: The Bank operates in PLN and foreign currencies across domestic and international markets, offering comprehensive services (retail, private, corporate, asset management, brokerage) backed by strong capital/liquidity and high risk management standards. The 2021–2024 business strategy (Responsible Bank. Modern Banking) concluded in 2024; a new strategy is being developed. The ESG Strategy (Responsible Bank Supporting Sustainable Development), adopted June 25, 2021, extends the Responsibility pillar and is structured around:
  - Environment: increase sustainable financing, support energy transition/low-carbon economy, target own carbon neutrality by 2030, participate in government/EU programs.
  - Social Responsibility: support societal and economic development, inclusion, education, partnerships; promote environmental awareness; back growth/innovation of Polish enterprises; develop electronic/mobile payments with tech partners.
  - Corporate Governance: ethical business integrating ESG; promote development, diversity, equality, inclusion; ensure transparent policies and strong governance; invest in people via training, development, and open dialogue.
  Note: ESG Strategy pillars are not directly linked to impacts/risks/opportunities identified in the double materiality analysis.

- Business model and customer segmentation:
  - Retail and Private Banking: individuals, high-net-worth clients, and micro-enterprises served via branches, partner outlets, and digital/remote channels; private banking provides investment advisory.
  - Corporate Banking: SMEs served by relationship managers and product specialists through Business Customer Centres, Corporate Centres, and retail branches.
  - Corporate and Investment Banking: large corporates, public sector, financial institutions, and commercial real estate clients served by relationship managers with specialist support.

- Value chain mapping (Banking sector):
  - Upstream: financial infrastructure (payment systems, clearing houses, deposit systems), card networks (Visa, Mastercard), tech/infrastructure providers, utilities, telecoms; focus on continuity, reliability, availability, and user-friendly solutions.
  - Organisation (entity operations): retail, business, corporate, capital markets, investment banking; underpinned by risk management, finance, HR, and strategy; emphasis on technology/operations development, employee competencies, and organisational culture.
  - Downstream: services to individuals (personal banking, loans, savings), public sector (public finance management, bond issuance), corporates (loans, treasury, transaction services), and financial counterparties (banks, supranationals); supported by digital platforms, distribution network, and marketing.

- Stakeholder engagement and double materiality:
  - Communication governed by Bank Pekao Information Policy Principles for investors, analysts, media, and customers.
  - 2024 materiality assessment identified key stakeholder groups via value chain mapping and inputs from 18 business units to build a Stakeholder Map.
  - Double materiality survey (42 questions across environmental, social, governance plus an open question) conducted per CSRD; respondents: 78% internal (employees and subsidiaries) and 22% external; non-employee workers classified as own human resources were not included.
  - Stakeholders perceived the strongest positive impacts in the social area and strongest negative impacts in corporate governance; aggregated results presented to the Steering Committee and ESG Council.

structure.title: Stakeholder Interests and Opinions [SBM-2]
structure.heading: 13.1.3.2 Stakeholder Interests and Opinions [SBM-2]
structure.start_phrase: We place great importance on managing relationships with stakeholders, taking their needs into account , and ensuring equal access to information.
structure.summary:
- The excerpt is from the 2024 Report on the activities of Bank Pekao S.A. Group and outlines the Group’s organizational foundations and stakeholder-focused ESG approach.
- Organizational foundations: strong emphasis on risk management, finance, HR, strategy, continuous development of technology and operations, employee competencies, and organizational culture.
- Value chain focus (Downstream): services for individual clients (retail banking, loans, savings), public sector (public finance management, bond issuance), and corporate clients (commercial loans, treasury, transaction services), plus financial counterparties (banks, supranationals), supported by advanced digital platforms, distribution networks, and marketing.
- Stakeholder governance and communication: managed under Bank Pekao’s Information Policy Principles to ensure transparency and equal access to information.
- Stakeholder identification and mapping: conducted in 2024 via a materiality assessment; 18 business units contributed to a Group-wide Stakeholder Map for the credit institutions value chain.
- Double materiality analysis per CSRD: stakeholder survey with 42 questions (1 general, 18 environmental, 14 social, 5 governance, plus open-ended); respondents were 78% internal (employees, subsidiaries) and 22% external; non-employee own workers excluded. Stakeholders perceived the strongest positive impacts in social areas and the strongest negative in corporate governance; aggregated results reported to the Steering Committee and ESG Council.
- Ongoing stakeholder engagement: commitment to open communication and actions to enhance positive impacts and reduce negative ones.
- Summary of relationships with key stakeholder groups:
  - Shareholders/strategic owner: transparent reporting, strategy execution, value creation, adherence to regulations, robust investor relations.
  - Customers: quality products/services, consumer fair practices, fund security, multi-channel access, clear offers/contract terms, feedback mechanisms, responsible marketing.
  - Employees and unions: job stability, development and training, clear goals, fair pay/benefits, work-life balance, remote work options, health initiatives, structured dialogue with social partners.
  - Regulators/supervisors: compliance and active cooperation in shaping market rules and best practices.
  - Central banks/financial institutions: dialogue on ESG projects, experience exchange, market practice development.
  - Pekao Group entities: group-level policy/procedure implementation and best-practice sharing.
  - Suppliers/partners: transparent procurement, timely contract execution, promotion of good purchasing practices; involvement in charitable/sponsorship and climate-related actions.
  - Industry organizations/competitors: transparency on non-financial reports, results, strategy; market monitoring and trend analysis to build best practices.
  - Natural environment: support for social/environmental projects, employee engagement in environmental initiatives, efforts to reduce environmental impacts and provide environmental education.
- New Business and ESG Strategy: driven by evolving sustainability regulations, supervisory recommendations, market practices, and stakeholder expectations; aims to integrate ESG into procedures and product/credit/investment processes; to be published in 2025, built on Baseline Analysis plus macro and sector scenarios; developed with Management Board involvement and subject to Management and Supervisory Board approval; goal is strong stakeholder relationships.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities: 26 ESRS-aligned topics plus 4 additional significant topics identified via double materiality; impact assessment considered type (positive/negative), locus (value chain—mainly credit portfolio/organization), timing (actual/potential), and time horizons (short: 1 year; medium: 1–5 years; long: >5 years).
- Financial materiality analysis: assessed opportunities and risks related to the business model, value chain, strategy, and decision-making across the same three time horizons.

structure.title: Material Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities and Their Interrelation with Strategy and Business Model [SBM-3]
structure.heading: 13.1.3.3 Material Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities and Thei r Interrelation with Strategy and Business Model [SBM-3]
structure.start_phrase: As a result of the double materiality analysis, we identified 26 topics aligned with ESRS and four add itional topics (not covered under ESRS) that Pekao Group significantly impacts (impact materiality) or that significantly affect t he Group’s operations (financial materiality).
structure.summary:
- Stakeholder engagement overview: identifies key groups (central banks and financial institutions, Pekao Group entities, suppliers and business partners, industry organizations and competitors, and the natural environment) with specific communication tools, topics (e.g., ESG projects, cooperation, market practices), and actions (e.g., transparent procurement, timely contract execution, employee environmental initiatives).
- New Business and ESG Strategy: Bank Pekao plans a combined Business and ESG Strategy to be published in 2025, integrating ESG into product, credit, and investment processes in response to regulation, supervisory recommendations, market practices, and stakeholder expectations; developed with Management Board oversight, based on baseline analysis and sector/macroeconomic scenarios, and aiming to strengthen stakeholder relationships.
- Double materiality results [SBM-3]: 26 ESRS-aligned topics plus four additional material issues identified; impacts assessed by type, place in value chain, and time horizons (short, medium, long); financial materiality assessed for risks/opportunities across the same horizons and value chain locations.
- Key risk and opportunity conclusions: no material risks to the business model, strategy, or value chain identified for the current, medium, or long term; short‑term elevated risk of potential UOKiK fines linked to consumer protection matters; long‑term potential increase in credit risk tied to financing companies with low tax transparency; climate risk analysis indicates no threats to resilience, though a formal climate resilience assessment was not performed.
- Climate topics (E1): positive impacts via financing adaptation and mitigation projects (renewables, energy efficiency), with related revenue opportunities; acknowledgment of exposure to high‑emission sectors through the credit portfolio; sustainable finance framework supports green and social financing.
- Workforce topics (S1): generally positive impacts on secure employment, working hours, fair pay, social dialogue, freedom of association, collective bargaining (>70% coverage), work‑life balance, OHS, training, anti‑harassment measures, diversity, and GDPR‑compliant employee privacy; noted potential negative impact from automation/AI on job stability; existing gender pay gap with actions underway to reduce it.
- Consumers and end users (S4): positive impacts in privacy protection, access to high‑quality information, personal financial safety, non‑discrimination (including sign‑language advisory), access to products/services, responsible marketing, and financial education; identified short‑term regulatory risk (UOKiK) related to consumer protection issues.
- Business conduct (G1): strong corporate culture, whistleblower protection, supplier code of conduct with ESG verification, anti‑corruption policy and training, incident monitoring; tax transparency cooperation (CRS, FATCA) with recognition of related downstream credit risk; robust cybersecurity and data protection practices supporting sector stability and trust.
- Management of impacts, risks, and opportunities [IRO‑1]: first‑time double materiality assessment conducted in 2024 under a Steering Committee with Management Board involvement; aligned with CSRD/ESRS; integrated with the risk management function including ESG materiality thresholds.
- Methodology and stakeholder process: four phases (value chain mapping; analysis and stakeholder dialogue for impact materiality; financial materiality assessment; matrix synthesis and topic list); used expert input, internal/external stakeholder surveys, management interviews, and benchmarking; sectors identified per ESRS/EFRAG with a >10% revenue threshold; nine key stakeholder groups determined; impact assessment considered timing and scale, among other factors.

structure.title: Description of the Process for Identifying and Assessing Material Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities [IRO-1]
structure.heading: 13.1.3.4.1 Description of the Process for Identifying and Asse ssing Material Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities [IRO-1]
structure.start_phrase: As part of the preparation for this Report, we cond ucted for the first time a double materiality asses sment to identify key stakeholder groups relevant to Bank Pekao S.A. and the entire Capital Group, as well as material impac ts, risks, and opportunities related to sustainability issues.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Bank Pekao S.A. Group’s first double materiality assessment under CSRD/ESRS, its governance, methodology, findings, and how disclosures map to ESRS requirements.
- Governance and integration: Process led by a cross‑functional project team under a Steering Committee (department directors and Management Board reps), with active involvement of the risk management unit to align ESG risks/opportunities with the existing risk framework and set materiality thresholds.
- Methodology and phases:
  - Identification of key business sectors (EFRAG sector classification; threshold >10% of revenue) and value chain mapping.
  - Analysis of existing data (benchmarks vs. peers, industry reports, ESG ratings) and stakeholder dialogue for impact materiality.
  - Financial materiality assessment of risks and opportunities across three time horizons.
  - Matrix analysis to finalize ESG topics material to the Group.
- Stakeholder engagement: Assessment of 16 stakeholder groups on two parameters (Group’s impact on them and their interest in the Group), resulting in nine key stakeholder groups; inputs included expert assessments, structured management interviews, and anonymous internal/external surveys.
- Impact materiality: Comprehensive assessment across ESRS themes using criteria such as timing, scale, probability, extent, and reversibility; scoring on a 1–5 scale; topics deemed material if exceeding a defined threshold and validated through preliminary analyses.
- Financial materiality: Identification and scoring (probability and financial impact) of 151 risks/opportunities across current, ≤5 years, and >5 years; topics considered financially material if any associated risk/opportunity scored above threshold in any horizon; outcome includes four financially material ESRS topics plus one additional topic.
- Climate (ESRS E1):
  - Physical risks assessed using a high‑emissions scenario (SSP5‑8.5); financial impact analysis (E1‑9) currently qualitative under transitional provisions, with quantitative elements published separately (e.g., capital adequacy reports).
  - Transition risks aligned with a Paris‑consistent pathway (SSP1‑1.9) considering regulatory trends and reputation pressures; ongoing quantitative work (e.g., sectoral credit quality, collateral energy efficiency) and a forthcoming transformation plan to deepen targets and methods.
- Other environmental topics:
  - E2 (Pollution): Reviewed own operations and portfolio; no local environmental impacts identified; no affected‑community consultations.
  - E3 (Water): Reviewed operational use (offices/branches) and portfolio; no material impacts; no local consultations.
  - E4 (Biodiversity): Assessed own sites, portfolio, and value chain; no material impacts; related risks noted but no transition/physical risk assessment; no systemic risk or ecosystem services assessment due to the nature of banking services.
  - E5 (Circular economy): Reviewed own operations and portfolio; no material impacts; no consultations.
- Key outcomes:
  - Sector classification: Credit Institutions within the Financial Institutions macro‑sector.
  - Nine key stakeholder groups identified.
  - 26 ESRS‑aligned topics deemed material with 26 sub‑topics, predominantly social (19) focusing on own workforce (13) and consumers/end users (6); environmental materiality centered on climate change mitigation and adaptation; governance materiality includes organizational culture, whistleblowing, supplier management, and anti‑corruption/anti‑bribery.
  - Four additional material topics beyond ESRS.
  - Results approved by the ESG Council.
- ESRS compliance mapping: Inclusion of a table that links each ESRS disclosure requirement to specific report sections (covering ESRS 2, governance GOV‑1–GOV‑5, strategy/business model SBM‑1–SBM‑3, IRO‑1–IRO‑2), and detailed climate change (E1) disclosures on transition plan, policies, actions/resources, targets, energy use/mix, and Scope 1–3 and total GHG emissions.

structure.title: Disclosure Requirements under ESRS Covered by the Entity’s Sustainability Statement [IRO-2]
structure.heading: 13.1.3.5 Disclosure Requirements under ESRS Covered by the E ntity’s Sustainability Statement [IRO-2]
structure.start_phrase: Disclosure Requirements under ESRS Covered by the E ntity’s Sustainability Statement.
structure.summary:
- Scope and outcome of ESRS double materiality analysis: Bank Pekao S.A. Group classified as Credit Institutions; 9 stakeholder groups; 26 ESRS-aligned topics deemed material (mostly social: own workforce and consumers/end users), with environmental materiality limited to climate change mitigation and adaptation, and five governance topics (culture, whistleblowing, supplier management, anti-corruption/bribery); four additional non-ESRS topics; approved by the ESG Council.
- Environmental topics E3, E4, E5: Assessments found no material impacts on water/marine resources, biodiversity/ecosystems, or circular economy; limited risk identification for biodiversity without transition/physical risk assessment; no community consultations due to non-materiality.
- ESRS compliance mapping: Comprehensive tables linking each disclosure requirement (ESRS 2 GOV/SBM/IRO; E1–E5; S1–S4; G1) to report sections, with explicit omissions/“N/A” where not applicable or not reported.
- Cross-regulatory alignment: Data points cross-referenced to SFDR, CRR/CRD Pillar 3 disclosures, the Benchmark Regulation, and the European Climate Law, showing where metrics and targets correspond.
- Social disclosures (ESRS S1): Policies, engagement, grievance mechanisms, targets, workforce characteristics, diversity, fair pay, social protection, training, OHS, work-life balance, gender pay and remuneration, and human rights incidents; disability metrics marked N/A. S2 (value-chain workers) and S3 (affected communities) largely N/A; S4 (consumers/end users) partly covered.
- Governance and business conduct (ESRS G1): Roles and responsibilities, due diligence, sustainability in incentives, supplier relationship management, anti-corruption/bribery controls and incidents, payment practices; political influence/lobbying marked N/A.
- Additional topics beyond ESRS: Financial education, cybersecurity/data security, tax transparency, and sustainable finance.
- Climate change (ESRS E1) transition planning: No formal transition plan as of 31 Dec 2024; 2024 work to measure financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) and adoption of Decarbonisation Guidelines for the credit portfolio; plan to formalize a transition plan within two years.
- Financed emissions baseline and pathway: PCAF-based estimate of 5.4 MtCO2e (Scopes 1–2 of financed entities) for a EUR 34.0bn portfolio (31 Dec 2023); main asset classes covered; largest contributors are corporate loans, unlisted equity, and project finance (60% of financed emissions); key sectors: power generation and iron/steel; alignment with IEA Net Zero (1.5°C) scenario; intent to set 2030 and 2050 targets and update regularly; focus on eco-efficiency in own operations and financing Poland’s energy transition, with greatest leverage via strategic customers (>65% sector exposure).

structure.title: Transition Plan for Climate Change Mitigation [E1-1]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.1 Transition Plan for Climate Change Mitigation [E1-1 ]
structure.start_phrase: As of the reporting date, 31 December 2024, we did not have a transition plan for climate change mitig ation.
structure.summary:
- Scope and context: Environmental Information, Climate Change (ESRS E1), focusing on the transition plan for climate mitigation (E1-1) and policies for managing climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities (E1-2).
- Transition plan status:
  - No formal transition plan as of 31 December 2024.
  - 2024 analytical work launched to calculate and assess materiality of financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) for credit and investment portfolios.
  - Decarbonisation Guidelines for the Pekao Group’s Credit Portfolio adopted by end-2024 to guide further actions and inform the business model transformation plan.
- Scenario alignment and targets approach:
  - Work anchored in the IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) 1.5°C scenario.
  - Global emissions trajectory assumed: −38% by 2030 and −100% by 2050 vs. 2020.
  - Quantitative decarbonisation targets for 2030 and 2050 to be set based on analysis; plan to use best available data and production-intensity metrics to align with a 1.5°C pathway; periodic plan updates.
- Financed emissions measurement:
  - PCAF methodology applied to financed emissions (absolute and intensity).
  - As of 31 December 2023: portfolio exposure EUR 34,014 million; financed emissions 5.4 MtCO2e (Scope 1 and 2 of financed entities).
  - Asset classes covered: listed shares and corporate bonds; corporate loans and unlisted equity; project finance; commercial real estate; mortgage loans; vehicle loans.
  - Emissions concentration: corporate loans, unlisted equity, and project finance = 60% of financed emissions.
  - Most material sectors: electricity generation; iron and steel.
- Strategic levers and actions:
  - Primary levers: eco-efficiency in own operations; financing Poland’s energy transition; tailored offers for corporate, business, and retail clients.
  - Highest leverage with strategic clients representing >65% of sector exposure.
  - Despite no science-based quantitative targets yet, actions are embedded in ESG Strategy KPIs; no attribution of actions to emission reductions during the reporting period due to lack of set targets.
  - Forward plan: selective growth—scale low-emission financing; limit exposure to high-emission entities; tailor approach to clients’ transition maturity; assess locked-in emissions; integrate plan into corporate strategy and financial plans; periodic regulatory disclosures.
  - Governance: Decarbonisation guidelines approved by the ESG Council; the Bank is not excluded from EU Paris-aligned benchmarks.
- Policies and governance (E1-2):
  - No single overarching climate policy; climate factors integrated across internal regulations (e.g., ESG Strategy, Supplier Code of Ethics, transaction identification/monitoring guidelines).
  - External standards and market norms inform internal regulations where applicable.
  - Stakeholders: internal (employees, unions); external (shareholders, customers, regulators/supervisors, suppliers, partners).
  - No thematic consultations for setting objectives, but ongoing dialogue via established channels; relevant operational units involved in drafting.
  - Internal regulations are mostly non-public, with key elements of select documents published.
  - Planned development of a coordinated regulatory document to systematize management of climate impacts, risks, and opportunities across the Bank.

structure.title: Policies Related to Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation [E1-2]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.2.1 Policies Related to Climate Change Mitigation and A daptation [E1-2]
structure.start_phrase: At our Bank, climate aspects are integrated into th e internal regulatory framework and implemented acr oss various operational areas as sustainable development factors.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Bank Pekao S.A. Group’s climate-related governance, policies, risk management, and financing approach within its 2024 activities report, centered on its ESG Strategy and transition planning.
- Decarbonisation approach:
  - No science-based quantitative decarbonisation targets set yet; key levers defined and tracked via ESG Strategy KPIs.
  - During the period, actions were not quantitatively linked to achieved emission reductions in financing or own operations.
  - Forthcoming selective growth strategy to increase low‑emission financing and limit exposure to high‑emission entities, tailored to clients’ transition maturity.
  - Analysis of locked‑in emissions planned; integration of the transition plan into overall strategy and financial plans with periodic regulatory disclosures.
  - ESG Council approved decarbonisation guidelines and oversees implementation; the Bank is not excluded from EU climate benchmarks aligned with the Paris Agreement.
- Management of impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - Climate aspects integrated across internal regulations rather than a single climate policy; goals and procedures dispersed (ESG Strategy, Supplier Code of Ethics, internal monitoring guidelines).
  - External standards and best practices inform regulations; key stakeholders identified and engaged through ongoing dialogue, though no formal thematic consultations for rule‑setting.
  - Plan to develop a unifying regulatory document to coordinate climate impact, risk, and opportunity management across the Bank.
- ESG Strategy 2021–2024:
  - Predates ESRS, so structure may not fully align with new regulatory characteristics.
  - Own operations: establish Scope 1, 2, and 3 (supply chain) carbon footprint measurement; implement eco‑efficiency in facilities and reduce material use.
  - Lending/investment: reduce exposure to high‑emission activities (e.g., new coal/lignite mining and coal‑fired generation) while increasing financing of low‑emission projects supporting Poland’s energy transition; started calculating financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15) in 2024.
  - Business opportunities: financing renewables (wind, biogas, PV), low‑emission technologies and transport, green construction, and participation in government/EU transition programs.
- Own operations and supply chain policies:
  - Policy on Energy Consumption Optimisation (2019) guides energy use and property/equipment practices; overseen by the Real Estate Department.
  - Procurement Policy (2024) integrates ESG into purchasing; Supplier Code of Ethics requires supplier acknowledgement and climate‑related practices.
  - No formal internal regulations for strategic decarbonisation targets (Scope 1/2) yet; to be established alongside target adoption and the business model transition plan.
- Credit and investment portfolio risk management:
  - Credit Risk Strategy (Supervisory Board‑approved) and Credit Risk Policy (Management Board‑approved) embed ESG/climate risk, define risk appetite, and guide integration in lending across segments.
  - General stance: no new financing and limited ongoing financing for high‑emission sectors (coal/lignite power and supporting activities), with exceptions for transformational projects.
  - Detailed segment regulations identify high/medium‑emission portfolios, outline green versus brown financing, and support portfolio steering and education.
  - From 2024, a formal ESG risk procedure (aligned with KNF, EBA, and best practices) defines identification, measurement, and control; sets a strategic limit for green financing; introduces indicators to monitor exposure to fossil fuel‑related financing and GHG intensity in corporate financing; sets ESG reporting requirements for Group companies. Ownership lies with the Risk Strategy and Development and ESG Department.
- Sustainable Finance Framework (since 2023):
  - Governs sustainable bond issuance and defines criteria for environmentally/socially sustainable corporate and investment banking transactions.
  - Aligned with EU Taxonomy technical criteria and ICMA/LMA principles; received a second‑party opinion from Sustainalytics.
  - Responsibilities span Corporate Banking, Markets & Investment Banking, Business Banking, and the Brokerage House.
- Green product offering:
  - Retail/consumer: aligned with Poland’s Energy Efficiency Law (energy savings target and certificate system through 2030).
  - Businesses: utilize European Funds for a Modern Economy under the BGK framework.
  - Corporate: governed by the Sustainable Finance Framework in line with ICMA/LMA standards.
- Governance and disclosures:
  - ESG Council (including Management Board members) monitors strategy implementation; outcomes communicated in annual non‑financial reports; selected documents available on the Bank’s website.
  - Upcoming section notes that actions/resources were set pre‑ESRS and may not fully align with new reporting requirements.

structure.title: Actions and Resources Related to Climate Policy [E1-3]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.2.2 Actions and Resources Related to Climate Policy [E1 -3]
structure.start_phrase: Both the strategic objectives and the related actio ns were established prior to the introduction of re gulatory requirements under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards.
structure.summary:
- ESG risk governance: In 2024 the Bank formalized an ESG risk management procedure overseen by the Vice President for Risk and owned by the Risk Strategy and Development and ESG Department, aligning with KNF, EBA and market best practices. It sets processes for ESG risk identification, measurement and control; introduces a strategic limit on green financing (share in total portfolio); and establishes internal indicators to monitor high‑emission financing (fossil fuels, fossil‑based power) and GHG intensity in corporate financing. Responsibilities for implementation and Pekao Capital Group reporting are defined, and selected ESG risk appetite elements are disclosed externally.

- Sustainable Finance Framework (since 2023): Governs corporate and investment banking, sets conditions for classifying client transactions as environmentally or socially sustainable, and provides the issuance framework for sustainable bonds. It covers project selection, proceeds management, allocation and impact reporting for EMTN green bonds. It aligns with EU Taxonomy technical criteria and leading standards (ICMA Green/Social/Sustainability Bond Principles, LMA Green/Social Loan Principles). Sustainalytics provided an SPO. Execution responsibilities span Corporate Banking, Markets & Investment Banking, Business Banking, and Pekao Brokerage.

- Green product enablement: 
  - Retail/consumer lending guided by Poland’s Energy Efficiency Law (2016) and national energy‑saving targets through 2030.
  - Business clients supported via European Funds for a Modern Economy (BGK Act).
  - Corporate financing governed by the Sustainable Finance Framework aligned with ICMA/LMA standards.

- Climate policy actions (ESRS E1 context): Objectives and actions were set pre‑ESRS; therefore, targets are not fully ESRS‑aligned and lack quantified decarbonization pathways. No incidents of significant harm to third parties were identified, so no remediation was required.

- Own operations: CAPEX/OPEX are not Taxonomy-eligible under EU 2021/2178 and are financially insignificant; the Bank applies a prudent approach to avoid misclassification/greenwashing. 2024 initiatives included LED retrofits, energy optimization (contracted power reductions), UPS replacements, decommissioning backup connections, efficient HVAC, reactive power compensation analyses, device standby automation, water pressure reducers/aerators, and energy‑efficient appliances. The Bank purchased electricity with guarantees of origin for 100% of contracted volume (certificate confirming 28,000 MWh from wind in 2024), advanced digital process changes, and refreshed the fleet with EURO 6 and hybrid vehicles.

- Credit and investment activities: Core sustainability impact delivered via financing Poland’s energy transition and sustainability‑linked products for corporate, business and retail clients. Given the absence of financed‑emissions targets and pre‑ESRS design, 2024 financing is not linked to quantified emission reductions, though considered a driver of portfolio decarbonization.

- 2024 sustainable financing results (corporate, investment, business):
  - Green financing: approx. PLN 13.738 billion.
  - New sustainable financing: PLN 12.697 billion.
  - Customer bond issuance financing: PLN 20.92 billion.
  - EU Taxonomy‑aligned exposures: CAPEX KPI PLN 3.173 billion; TURNOVER KPI PLN 2.092 billion.
  - Other: corporate client carbon footprint calculator launched; BGK guarantee limits—Biznesmax plus working capital PLN 136m, investment PLN 204m; Ekomax PLN 250m.

- Green bond allocation: First allocation report (Nov 2024) for the 2023 EMTN green bond issue (EUR 500m). As of Oct 15, 2024, 33 projects totaling EUR 526.84m were included, fully allocating proceeds within a year.

- Retail ESG offering:
  - Express Loan for EKO purposes up to PLN 100,000 with 0% commission and reduced margin for qualifying green uses; gross carrying amount PLN 281m as of 31.12.2024.
  - EKODOM residential loan with reduced margin for energy‑saving installations; gross carrying amount PLN 204m as of 31.12.2024.
  - From Nov 1, 2024, energy performance criteria assessed at mortgage application; meeting EP threshold yields lower margin; EPC data aggregated for statistics.

- Metrics and targets:
  - Quarterly internal supervision of ESG Strategy progress (2021–2024). No ESRS E1‑aligned GHG reduction targets for the strategy period; metrics focus on financial and exposure measures rather than CO2e.
  - Targets aim to reduce transition risk from high‑emission sector exposure and seize climate‑related business opportunities.
  - Long‑term own‑operations and supply‑chain GHG reduction ambition set for 2030 (beyond ESG Strategy horizon); no climate‑neutrality commitment or interim milestones.
  - Definitions and methodologies draw on EU Taxonomy, ICMA, LMA, EU GBS, and CBI; not externally validated.
  - No separate environmental targets were established beyond green eligibility criteria; external stakeholders were not involved in target setting.
  - All quantitative portfolio financing targets for 2021–2024 were achieved, exceeding minimum cumulative thresholds.

structure.title: Monitoring the Results of Actions Derived from the Climate Policy
structure.heading: 13.2.1.3.2 Monitoring the Results of Actions Derived from the Climate Policy
structure.start_phrase: The results of implementing the Bank’s climate poli cy objectives and directions set out in the ESG Strategy are subject to quarterly internal supervision, in accordance with the provisions of the internal regulations governin g the processes of developing and monitoring the ESG Strategy .
structure.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpts from Bank Pekao S.A. Group’s 2024 activity report covering ESRS E1 disclosures on metrics, targets, energy use, and GHG emissions (sections 13.2.1.3–13.2.1.4).
- ESG Strategy (2021–2024) governance and approach:
  - Quarterly internal monitoring of climate policy and ESG Strategy performance.
  - No ESRS E1-aligned portfolio decarbonization targets set for 2021–2024; targets focused on financial/portfolio composition and business opportunities rather than CO2e reductions.
  - Long-term own-operations ambition: climate neutrality by 2030 for Scope 1 and 2; no organizational-level neutrality or reduction targets set within the Strategy horizon.
  - Targets and metrics predate ESRS; designed using EU Taxonomy, ICMA Principles, LMA Principles, EU Green Bond Standard (Reg. 2023/2631), and Climate Bonds Initiative; peer analysis used; no external validation and no external stakeholder involvement in target setting.
  - Baseline year 2020; no interim milestones during 2021–2024 and no metric changes.
- Portfolio-related goals and outcomes (2021–2024):
  - New sustainable projects financed: PLN 12.697bn (target > PLN 8bn).
  - Share of green financing: 7.90% (target > 4%; baseline 3.2%).
  - Share of high-emission financing: 0.69% (target < 1%; baseline 1.3%).
  - ESG bond support: PLN 20.92bn mobilized vs. intention to exceed PLN 22bn.
  - Strategic step taken in 2024: calculation of financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) as the basis for setting future methodologies and timelines toward net‑zero financed emissions by 2050 (Paris-aligned 1.5°C pathway). Decarbonization directions adopted for energy generation and iron & steel sectors.
- Own operations emissions progress:
  - Scope 1 and 2 absolute emissions reduced from 69,790.9 tCO2e (2020 baseline) to 30,973 tCO2e (2024); climate neutrality target by 2030 maintained.
- Energy consumption and mix (E1‑5):
  - Reporting boundary aligned with GHG inventory; only final energy used by the Group; no offsets; self-generated renewable energy used internally only.
  - 2024 total energy consumption: 97,570.82 MWh (down from 119,327.41 MWh in 2023).
  - Fossil energy: 69,165.09 MWh; 71% of total (72% in 2023).
  - Renewable and low‑emission energy: 28,405.72 MWh; 29% of total (28% in 2023), including 28,352.02 MWh purchased renewables and 53.7 MWh self‑generated.
  - No nuclear; no renewable fuels (e.g., biomass) used; no energy intensity KPI disclosed due to non‑significant climate impact sector.
  - Use of guarantees of origin and PPAs; 29% of electricity from these arrangements.
- GHG emissions accounting (E1‑6):
  - Methodology: GHG Protocol Corporate Standard; Pekao Group boundary; not in EU ETS; data from internal consumption and official factors (KOBIZE, URE, DEFRA, suppliers); results in tCO2e; no biogenic emissions identified; no external calculation tools.
  - Scope 3 in 2024 includes only Category 15 (financed emissions). Materiality review found Categories 2, 3 (location-based), and 7 >0.1% of Category 15; plan to add Categories 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 13, and 14 in future years; remaining categories deemed immaterial or data-limited.

structure.title: Gross Greenhouse Gas Emissions for Scopes 1, 2, and 3 and Total Greenhouse Gas Emissions [E1-6]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.4 Gross Greenhouse Gas Emissions for Scopes 1, 2, and 3 and Total Greenhouse Gas Emissions [E1-6]
structure.start_phrase: To calculate greenhouse gas emissions under Scopes 1 and 2, we applied the methodology outlined in the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard.
structure.summary:
- Presents 2023–2024 energy consumption and mix for Bank Pekao S.A. Group:
  - Total energy use fell from 119,327 MWh (2023) to 97,571 MWh (2024).
  - Fossil energy declined to 69,165 MWh; fossil share moved from 72% to 71%.
  - Renewable share rose from 28% to 29%, mainly from purchased renewable electricity (28,352 MWh) plus 53.7 MWh of self-generated renewables.
  - The Group states it is not in a sector with significant climate impact; therefore, it does not break down fossil fuels by type and does not report energy intensity by revenue.

- Details greenhouse gas accounting approach (ESRS E1-6):
  - Scopes 1 and 2 calculated under the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard; not subject to EU ETS; no biogenic emissions; internal data with factors from KOBIZE, URE, DEFRA, and suppliers; no external calculation tools.
  - Uses guarantees of origin and PPAs; 29% of total electricity is from renewable sources.
  - Scope 3 in 2024 includes only Category 15 (Investments/financed emissions). An assessment found Categories 2, 3 (location-based), and 7 exceed 0.1% of Category 15; additional categories identified as relevant for future reporting: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14. Remaining categories deemed not relevant or lack reliable data.

- Financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) methodology and coverage:
  - Covers on-balance-sheet exposures of the Bank and key subsidiaries (Pekao Bank Hipoteczny, Pekao Leasing, Pekao Faktoring); excludes off-balance assets (e.g., investment funds).
  - Applies PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard across relevant asset classes: corporate financing (incl. project finance), motor vehicle loans/leasing, mortgage-backed loans (retail and commercial real estate), listed equity and corporate bonds, and sovereign debt.
  - Data sources include national building energy certificates, PCAF European databases, reported borrower emissions, Bloomberg, and Refinitiv.
  - Average PCAF data quality scores (lower is better): Business loans 4.64; Equity and bonds 4.02; Project finance 4.77; Commercial real estate 3.83; Retail real estate 4.00; Motor vehicle loans 3.96.
  - Coverage: 77.82% of on-balance financial assets; 40% of financed emissions based on primary data; motor vehicles portfolio not included due to unavailable data. Leasing is treated under Category 15 following market practice.

- Reported GHG emissions:
  - Scope 1 (tCO2e): 8,104 (2022), 8,121 (2023), 8,704 (2024) (+7% YoY).
  - Scope 2 location-based (tCO2e): 64,153 (2022), 33,529 (2023), 24,498 (2024) (73% of 2023).
  - Scope 2 market-based (tCO2e): 57,312 (2022), n/a (2023), 24,604 (2024).
  - Total Scopes 1+2 location-based (tCO2e): 72,257 (2022), 41,650 (2023), 32,382 (2024) (78% of 2023).
  - Total Scopes 1+2 market-based (tCO2e): 65,416 (2022), n/a (2023), 32,513 (2024).
  - Scope 3 Category 15 (tCO2e, 2024): 14,657,189 total; split between the Bank (11,809,197) and subsidiaries (2,847,993).
  - Provides separate Scope 1 and 2 figures for the Bank and subsidiaries.

- Emissions intensity relative to revenue:
  - Location-based: 0.00019% (2023) improving to 0.00014% (2024).
  - Market-based: not calculated (2023); 0.00014% (2024).
  - Net revenue defined as income from interest, commissions, and dividends per 2024 Financial Statements.

- Additional disclosures:
  - No greenhouse gas removal or emission reduction projects financed via carbon units within own operations (E1-7).
  - No internal carbon pricing system in use (E1-8).
  - As a first-time ESRS reporter, the Group omits disclosure on expected financial impacts of climate risks and opportunities (E1-9).

structure.title: Greenhouse Gas Removal Projects and Greenhouse Gas Emission Reduction Projects Financed through Carbon Emission Units [E1-7]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.5 Greenhouse Gas Removal Projects and Greenhouse Gas Emission Reduction Projects Financed through Carbon Emission Units [E1-7]
structure.start_phrase: The purpose of disclosing information on greenhouse gas removal and emission reduction projects financ ed through carbon emission units is to provide insight into the unit’ s actions aimed at permanently removing or actively supporting the removal of greenhouse gases from the atmosphere, potentially w ith a view to achieving emission neutrality targets .
structure.summary:
- Presents Table 10 on greenhouse gas (GHG) emission intensity relative to revenue for Bank Pekao S.A.:
  - Location-based method: 0,00019% (2023) and 0,00014% (2024) t CO2e per net revenue.
  - Market-based method: not calculated in 2023; 0,00014% (2024) t CO2e per net revenue.
  - Net income defined as income from interest, commissions, and dividends per the Bank’s 2024 Financial Statements.
- Discloses that the Bank and Group do not undertake or actively support GHG removal or emission reduction projects financed through carbon emission units (E1-7), due to lack of control and non-engagement within own operations.
- States no use of internal carbon pricing systems and no participation in CO2 emission trading; thus, disclosure on internal carbon pricing (E1-8) is not applicable.
- Notes the use of the first-time reporting exemption under ESRS to omit disclosure of expected financial impacts of significant physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities (E1-9).

structure.title: Establishment of internal carbon emission pricing [E1-8]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.6 Establishment of internal carbon emission pricing [ E1-8]
structure.start_phrase: The subject of disclosure is information on whether the Pekao Group uses systems for establishing inte rnal carbon dioxide emission prices, and if so, how they assist in deci sion-making and encourage the implementation of cli mate-related policies and goals.
structure.summary:
- Part of Bank Pekao S.A. Group’s 2024 activity report focused on climate metrics and ESRS disclosures.
- Presents greenhouse gas emission intensity relative to revenue:
  - Location-based emissions per net revenue decreased from 0.00019% (2023) to 0.00014% (2024).
  - Market-based emissions per net revenue were not calculated in 2023; reported at 0.00014% in 2024.
  - “Net income” for this metric is defined as income from interest, commissions, and dividends, aligned with the Bank’s 2024 Financial Statements.
- E1-7 (GHG removal and reduction projects via carbon units): Not applicable; neither the Bank nor the Group conducts such projects within their own operations, and any capital involvement in the value chain lacks control required to count as active support.
- E1-8 (Internal carbon pricing): Not applicable; the Bank and Group do not engage in CO2 emission trading and do not use internal carbon pricing systems.
- E1-9 (Expected financial impacts of climate risks and opportunities): Omitted under the first-time ESRS reporting option per Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772, Annex C.

structure.title: Expected Financial Impacts of Significant Physical and Transition Risks and Potential Climate-Related Opportunities [E1-9]
structure.heading: 13.2.1.7 Expected Financial Impacts of Significant Physical and Transition Risks and Potential Climate-Related Opportunities [E1-9]
structure.start_phrase: Pursuant to Annex C to Commission Delegated Regulat ion (EU) 2023/2772 of 31 July 2023, units preparing their reports in accordance with ESRS requirements for the first tim e have the option to omit the information included in E1-9.
structure.summary:
- Presents greenhouse gas emission intensity relative to net revenue: location-based intensity decreased from 0.00019% in 2023 to 0.00014% in 2024; market-based method was not calculated in 2023 and is 0.00014% in 2024. Net revenue for this metric is defined as income from interest, commissions, and dividends per the Bank’s 2024 Financial Statements.
- States that the Bank and Group do not conduct or actively support greenhouse gas removal or emission reduction projects financed through carbon units (E1-7), including where there may be capital involvement without control.
- Notes no internal carbon pricing system is in place and disclosures on internal carbon pricing (E1-8) are not applicable, as the Bank and Group do not engage in carbon trading.
- Uses the ESRS first-time reporter option to omit disclosure of expected financial impacts of significant physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities (E1-9), per Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772.
- Introduces the EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852): criteria for environmentally sustainable activities (substantial contribution, do no significant harm, minimum social safeguards) and the six environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WMR, CE, PPC, BIO).
- Aligns with Bank Pekao’s 2021–2024 Business and ESG Strategies focused on: financing sustainable projects; supporting clients’ energy transition; and striving for climate neutrality by reducing emissions in operations and the supply chain.
- Outlines KPI disclosure requirements under the EU Taxonomy and related delegated regulations (2021/2178 as amended by 2023/2486; 2021/2139 as amended by 2023/2485), with 2024 disclosures covering KPIs for climate change mitigation (CCM) and climate change adaptation (CCA).

structure.title: EU Taxonomy
structure.heading: 13.2.2 EU Taxonomy
structure.start_phrase: Regulation (EU) 2020/852, known as the EU Taxonomy, was developed by the European Commission as part o f the European Green Deal.
structure.summary:
- Explains the EU Taxonomy framework (Regulation 2020/852) and its criteria: substantial contribution to one of six environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WMR, CE, PPC, BIO), Do No Significant Harm, and minimum social safeguards.
- Sets Bank Pekao’s ESG priorities (2021–2024): financing sustainable projects, supporting clients’ transition to a low‑carbon economy, and pursuing climate neutrality in own operations and value chain.
- Details regulatory basis and scope for 2024 disclosures (Delegated Regulations 2021/2178 and 2021/2139 with 2023 amendments), with mandatory KPIs for Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation.
- Defines the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and supplementary KPIs for off‑balance sheet items (financial guarantees and assets under management), including what is included/excluded in the GAR numerator and denominator (e.g., treatment of households, local governments, SMEs and non‑NFRD entities, derivatives, cash, central banks/governments, and trading book).
- Describes data sources and methodology: use of counterparties’ latest Taxonomy KPIs; handling of entities exempted from individual reporting; reliance on counterparties’ disclosures for minimum safeguards; and the Group’s plans to embed enhanced data collection into credit processes.
- Outlines household mortgage methodology: eligibility of residential mortgages; alignment tests under activity 7.7 (Acquisition and ownership of buildings) using Energy Performance Certificates and the national top‑15% PED thresholds (pre‑2021) or 10% below NZEB limits (post‑2020); DNSH screening for physical risks (floods, landslides); absence of renovation and motor‑vehicle loans in the retail book.
- Explains approach to local government financing: identification of use‑of‑proceeds loans, eligibility and DNSH assessment; limited documentation leading to disclosure as eligible (not aligned); no public housing financing identified; and revised treatment of unknown‑purpose exposures per Commission Notice C/2024/6691 (excluded from numerator, included in denominator).
- Presents consolidated quantitative disclosures as at 31 December 2024 per Annex VI templates:
  - Template 0 summary, including GAR stock (approximately 0.88%) and GAR flow (approximately 0.74%), plus KPIs for financial guarantees and managed assets.
  - Template 1 detailed GAR assets: breakdown by counterparty type (financial/non‑financial undertakings, households, local governments), taxonomy‑eligible vs. aligned amounts, enabling/transitional shares, and assets excluded/not covered; includes prior‑year (2023) comparatives for CCM and CCA.
  - Template 2 sectoral (NACE) breakdown of exposures and aligned amounts across objectives.
- Highlights from figures: taxonomy‑eligible assets are dominated by residential mortgages, with a smaller aligned portion due to energy‑performance documentation; aligned non‑financial corporate exposures appear across selected sectors (e.g., energy, rail transport, metals); off‑balance sheet positions include a limited share of taxonomy‑aligned financial guarantees and managed assets.

nodes.heading: 13.3.1 Own Workforce [ESRS S1]
nodes.start_phrase: Employee development is at the core of our ESG Stra tegy.
nodes.summary:
- Section 13.3 Social Aspects focuses on ESRS S1 – Own Workforce, centering on Bank employees who constitute 83% of the Group, with non-employee matters addressed when directly relevant.
- Scope of workforce covered includes: employees under employment contracts, individuals under civil law contracts (e.g., mandate/specific work), and non-employees providing services under B2B agreements.
- Employee development is a core pillar of the ESG Strategy, supported by a culture built on the values #prosto, #razem, #odważnie, #odpowiedzialnie and the 10 Key Principles of Team Management for leaders.
- Strategic aims include being an employer of choice (Top Employer award for the 14th consecutive year in 2024), operating as one strong team, attracting and retaining top talent, and ensuring conditions that drive motivation, satisfaction, and engagement.
- The Bank uses a double materiality assessment to identify material workforce impacts (referenced in section 13.1.3.4.1).
- Policies and governance for managing impacts, risks, and opportunities: adherence to labour law with equality and non-discrimination; application of internal policies, procedures, and rules to employees and civil law contractors; oversight by the President of the Management Board via the Human Resources Division.
